Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot causes water-soaked, dark brown or black angular spots on foliage and raised scab-like lesions on fruit.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked lesions that turn brown and necrotic
Leaves turning yellow and dropping prematurely
Raised, rough wart-like spots on peppers
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.causes: Warm, humid weather, splashing rain or overhead irrigation, infected seed.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Spray copper-based bactericides at first sign. Prune affected branches with disinfected tools.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: Apply Bacillus subtilis or copper soap spray. Remove diseased leaves immediately.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seed, rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years, avoid overhead irrigation.
precautions: Quarantine infected peppers and prune spotted leaves strictly during dry weather to avoid spreading bacteria.
Sanitize pruning shears, stakes, and gloves in 70% alcohol or 10% bleach between every single cut.
Immediately switch from overhead sprinklers to root-zone drip irrigation to eliminate bacterial water splash.
Do not touch, prune, or harvest damp foliage; bacterial cells readily travel on wet hands and clothing.
Bag and seal infected leaves in plastic; do NOT compost them, as bacteria can persist in organic matter.

Pepper__bell___healthy.description: The pepper bell leaf is vibrant, free from lesions, chlorosis, or pest infestation.
symptoms: Uniform green coloration
Smooth leaf margins and intact cuticle
Vigorous vegetative growth
Pepper__bell___healthy.causes: Optimal soil moisture, balanced nutrition, and good airflow.
Pepper__bell___healthy.treatment: No treatment required. Maintain current watering and fertilization schedules.
Pepper__bell___healthy.organic_treatment: Occasional foliar seaweed or compost tea to boost natural immunity.
Pepper__bell___healthy.prevention: Continue scouting weekly for early detection of aphid or mite vectors.
precautions: Conduct routine pest scouting twice weekly on leaf undersides for early signs of aphids or thrips.
Maintain consistent soil moisture; avoid waterlogging root zones which predisposes plants to root rot.
Keep soil mulched with clean straw or organic mulch to prevent soil-splash contact with lower leaves.
Ensure adequate plant spacing to maintain cross-ventilation as the pepper canopy expands.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight produces characteristic dark brown to black concentric ring spots (target board pattern) on mature leaves.
symptoms: Concentric rings forming target spots
Yellow halos surrounding lesions
Premature leaf senescence starting from lower canopy
Potato___Early_blight.causes: Alternating wet and dry periods, warm temperatures (24-29°C), nutrient stress.
Potato___Early_blight.treatment: Apply protective fungicides like chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin, or mancozeb.
Potato___Early_blight.organic_treatment: Copper octanoate fungicides and biofungicides (Trichoderma strains).
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium levels, practice 3-year crop rotation, eliminate volunteer potatoes.
precautions: Prune and discard all lower yellowing or target-spotted leaves immediately, starting from the ground up.
Apply a 3-inch layer of clean straw mulch around the base of potato plants to block soil-borne fungal spores.
Water exclusively at the base in early morning so accidental leaf moisture evaporates quickly in the sun.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which creates tender tissue vulnerable to Alternaria infection.
Disinfect digging and hilling tools after working in affected crop rows.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is the aggressive pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. Produces water-soaked lesions with pale white mildew underneath.
symptoms: Rapidly expanding water-soaked dark lesions
White fuzzy sporulation on leaf underside in high humidity
Foul odor and sudden collapse of foliage
Potato___Late_blight.causes: Cool, humid weather (15-20°C with relative humidity > 90%), prolonged leaf wetness.
Potato___Late_blight.treatment: Apply systemic fungicides (metalaxyl, mandipropamid) immediately upon warning.
Potato___Late_blight.organic_treatment: Preventative fixed copper sprays. Destroy and discard all infected canopy to stop spores.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Plant certified disease-free tubers, destroy cull piles, monitor local blight forecasting alerts.
precautions: ACT IMMEDIATELY (24-48 Hours): Late blight is an aggressive pathogen capable of destroying a crop within days.
Pull and bag severely infected plants immediately; seal in heavy plastic trash bags and bury or dispose off-site.
NEVER compost infected foliage or rotten tubers; fungal-like spores can overwinter and infect next year’s crop.
Alert neighboring growers or community allotments; airborne spores travel miles on cool, damp wind currents.
Wear gloves and disinfect boots with alcohol spray before walking into unaffected vegetable patches.
If harvest is approaching, cut and destroy vines 2 weeks prior to digging to prevent tuber rot infection.

Potato___healthy.description: Vigorous potato foliage with rich green color and robust canopy development.
symptoms: Lush green foliage without spots or necrosis
Normal leaflet expansion
Healthy stem structure
Potato___healthy.causes: Well-drained loose soil, appropriate hilling, balanced macronutrients.
Potato___healthy.treatment: Maintain healthy soil moisture and prevent soil compaction around tubers.
Potato___healthy.organic_treatment: Mulch with clean straw to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.
Potato___healthy.prevention: Scout lower leaves after rain events for early blight signs.
precautions: Ensure potato hills are adequately mounded to shield developing tubers from sunlight and spore wash.
Scout lower leaves after heavy rain or persistent morning fog for first signs of water-soaked spots.
Enforce a strict 3-year crop rotation avoiding solanaceous crops (potato, tomato, pepper, eggplant) in this bed.
Use only certified disease-free seed tubers for all subsequent plantings.

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.description: Causes circular to irregular greasy dark brown spots on leaves and stems, often with yellow halos.
symptoms: Dark, water-soaked circular lesions (<3mm)
Leaves become ragged as dead tissue falls out
Blister-like brown scabs on tomato fruits
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.causes: Splashing rain, overhead watering, high humidity (>85%) and temperatures around 25-30°C.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.treatment: Apply copper hydroxide mixed with mancozeb for synergistic bactericidal action.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: Bacteriophage treatments and copper soap sprays. Destroy heavily infected plants.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use drip irrigation, sanitize pruning shears with 70% alcohol, plant tolerant varieties.
precautions: Immediately halt all overhead sprinkling; water solely via drip or soaker hoses directly onto root beds.
Do not cultivate, weed, or touch plants while foliage is wet to prevent mechanical spreading of bacteria.
Prune lower diseased leaves using shears dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol between every single cut.
Collect and seal all diseased leaves and fallen fruit in airtight bags; discard away from garden beds.
Wash hands thoroughly with antibacterial soap and change gloves after handling infected plants.

Tomato_Early_blight.description: Produces distinctive concentric ring target spots on older foliage, eventually leading to defoliation.
symptoms: Target-like concentric ring brown lesions
Progressive yellowing spreading from leaf tips
Stem cankers near ground level
Tomato_Early_blight.causes: High humidity, heavy dew, warm sunny days alternating with rain.
Tomato_Early_blight.treatment: Spray with chlorothalonil, difenoconazole, or copper sulfate.
Tomato_Early_blight.organic_treatment: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or neem oil extracts applied preventatively.
Tomato_Early_blight.prevention: Prune bottom 12 inches of suckers/leaves, apply thick mulch to block soil splash.
precautions: Strip lower foliage 12 to 18 inches above soil level to create an anti-splash barrier against soil fungi.
Spread a 3-inch layer of clean wood chip or straw mulch under the entire canopy to cover bare soil.
Sanitize tomato stakes, cages, and trellises before reuse with a 10% household bleach solution.
Water early in the day so any inadvertent leaf splash evaporates within 1-2 hours.
Apply preventative bio-fungicide or copper spray to upper healthy foliage before upcoming rain storms.

Tomato_Late_blight.description: High-severity pathogen causing rapidly expanding grey-green greasy lesions that turn dark brown and can wipe out a crop within days.
symptoms: Large irregular dark water-soaked patches
White downy mold on leaf undersides in humid mornings
Greasy brown rot on green fruit
Tomato_Late_blight.treatment: Immediate systemic fungicide applications (cymoxanil, fluopicolide, or cyazofamid).
Tomato_Late_blight.organic_treatment: Preventative copper formulations before disease onset. Promptly pull and bag diseased plants.
Tomato_Late_blight.prevention: Allow wide plant spacing for airflow, never compost infected debris, use resistant hybrids (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Magic).
precautions: CRITICAL BIO-SECURITY ACTION: Late blight is an airborne epidemic threat that can wipe out entire tomato plots.
Bag and remove all plants with brown water-soaked lesions or white mold immediately during dry midday hours.
Do NOT compost diseased tissue; home compost piles do not reach temperatures needed to kill Phytophthora spores.
Apply systemic or protective copper spray to all surrounding asymptomatic plants immediately as a protective shield.
Sterilize stakes, cages, gloves, and footwear with disinfectant spray before visiting unaffected garden zones.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.description: Characterized by pale green to yellow chlorotic spots on leaf uppersides with velvety olive-brown mold underneath.
symptoms: Diffuse yellow patches on upper surface
Velvety olive to purple-brown sporulation on lower leaf surface
Premature leaf withering and curl
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.causes: High relative humidity (>85%) combined with warm greenhouse or sheltered tunnel environments.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.treatment: Apply fungicides such as trifloxystrobin or cyprodinil.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.organic_treatment: Improve greenhouse ventilation, use exhaust fans, apply sulfur or potassium bicarbonate.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.prevention: Keep greenhouse humidity below 80%, increase row spacing, prune dense foliage.
precautions: Maximize greenhouse or high-tunnel ventilation immediately; open louvers and run circulating fans continuously.
Keep relative humidity strictly below 85%; avoid closed, damp environments during warm afternoons.
Space plants wider apart and prune dense suckers to ensure sunlight penetrates deep into the inner canopy.
Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation; deliver water directly to the soil surface.
Remove and destroy leaves exhibiting fuzzy olive-brown mold patches underneath.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Common fungal disease causing numerous tiny circular spots with dark brown margins and sunken grey-tan centers with black specks.
symptoms: Multiple small (1.5-3mm) circular spots with dark borders and pale centers
Tiny black pycnidia visible inside spots under hand lens
Rapid lower foliage yellowing and drop
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.causes: Wet foliage from rainfall or overhead watering in warm weather (20-25°C).
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.organic_treatment: Liquid copper sprays and biological fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Stake and cage plants, apply 3 inches of mulch under canopy, avoid working with wet plants.
precautions: Remove diseased lower leaves showing dark-bordered speckled circular spots as soon as identified.
Apply thick mulch beneath plants to prevent rain from bouncing soil-borne Septoria spores onto leaves.
Avoid handling wet tomato foliage; spores are readily spread by hands, clothing, and tools.
Thoroughly clean up and discard all tomato plant residue at the end of the growing season.
Practice at least a 2-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants in that soil bed.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.description: Microscopic sap-sucking mites that produce stippled yellow foliage and fine silken webbing.
symptoms: Fine pale yellow speckled stippling on leaf surface
Silken webs stretching between leaf stems and tips
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, and drop
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.causes: Hot, dry, dusty weather; excessive synthetic pesticide use eliminating natural predators.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.treatment: Apply selective miticides (abamectin, bifenazate) covering leaf undersides thoroughly.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.organic_treatment: Spray insecticidal soap, horticultural mineral oil, or release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.prevention: Maintain overhead humidity in dry spells, wash dusty roadways, monitor leaf undersides weekly.
precautions: Isolate infested plants; spider mites easily crawl or blow onto adjacent host plants on gentle breezes.
Wash dusty pathways and surrounding soil; dry, dusty conditions drastically accelerate mite reproduction.
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic insecticides which kill natural beneficial predators like ladybugs and lacewings.
Spray leaf undersides thoroughly with a strong blast of water or insecticidal soap during cooler morning hours.
Introduce or protect predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) in enclosed or greenhouse settings.

Tomato__Target_Spot.description: Causes circular brown lesions with concentric rings and yellow halos that resemble early blight but affect fruit and upper canopy heavily.
symptoms: Zonate brown lesions with pale centers and subtle concentric rings
Sunken target lesions on both foliage and green fruit
Severe blighting in warm conditions
Tomato__Target_Spot.causes: High humidity, warm temperatures (20-28°C), and extended free leaf moisture.
Tomato__Target_Spot.treatment: Apply strobilurin fungicides or azoxystrobin + difenoconazole.
Tomato__Target_Spot.organic_treatment: Copper hydroxide sprays combined with removal of infected lower foliage.
Tomato__Target_Spot.prevention: Avoid planting near older infected solanaceous fields, maintain good field drainage.
precautions: Prune lower infected foliage and improve row spacing to reduce humidity pockets within the plant canopy.
Avoid overhead irrigation; keep foliage completely dry, particularly going into evening hours.
Remove and dispose of all fruit displaying sunken brown target rings to prevent fungal spore buildup.
Disinfect tomato trellis twine, stakes, and pruning tools with 70% alcohol or quaternary ammonium.
Rotate fields with non-host crops like corn or beans to break the soil inoculum cycle.

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.description: Devastating viral disease causing upward leaf curling, severe chlorosis, bushiness, and complete flower abortion.
symptoms: Cupped or rolled leaves with bright yellow margins
Interveinal chlorosis and reduced leaf blade size
Stunted bushy plant structure, flowers drop before fruit set
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.causes: Vector transmission by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.treatment: No viral cure exists. Systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) to suppress vector whiteflies.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.organic_treatment: Deploy yellow sticky traps, spray neem oil, rogue and bag infected plants immediately.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.prevention: Install 50-mesh insect netting in greenhouses, plant TYLCV-resistant hybrids, use reflective silver mulches.
precautions: CRITICAL VIRAL THREAT: TYLCV has no cure and is vectored rapidly by whiteflies to other crops.
Immediately rogue (uproot) and destroy infected plants showing stunted growth and upward leaf curl.
Place diseased plants directly into sealed plastic bags before transporting to avoid shaking whiteflies loose.
Deploy yellow sticky traps every 10-15 feet to monitor and capture adult whitefly populations.
Install 50-mesh anti-insect screens on greenhouse openings and apply reflective silver mulch in field beds.
Eliminate nearby weeds (like nightshade and mallow) which serve as wild virus and whitefly reservoirs.

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Extremely stable and infectious virus causing mottled dark and light green mosaic patterns, distorted shoestring leaves, and internal fruit browning.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves
Distorted, narrow, blistered or fern-like leaves
Stunted plants and mottled fruit with brown internal necrosis
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.causes: Mechanical transmission (pruning shears, worker hands, clothing, tobacco smoke residue).
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: No chemical cure. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.organic_treatment: Soak tools in 20% non-fat dry milk solution or 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) to deactivate viral particles.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Wash hands with soap before touching plants, forbid smoking near tomato crops, choose ToMV-resistant cultivars.
precautions: CRITICAL CONTAGION: Extremely stable virus transmitted by touch; survives for years on tools, seeds, and clothing.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and warm water or soak in 20% nonfat dry milk solution before and after touching plants.
STRICT NO SMOKING: Tobacco products carry related viruses and tobacco smoke residue can infect plants through touch.
Immediately discard infected mottled plants in household trash; NEVER compost or burn (smoke can carry particles).
Disinfect all pruning shears, trellises, and plant clips in a 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or bleach bath for 15 minutes.

Tomato_healthy.description: Vibrant tomato leaf with crisp dark green color, healthy trichomes (leaf hairs), and zero disease lesions.
symptoms: Deep green uniform color
Healthy serrated leaf margins and sturdy petiole
Active photosynthesis and vigorous shoot growth
Tomato_healthy.causes: Proper balance of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, consistent watering, and adequate sunlight.
Tomato_healthy.treatment: Continue standard cultural practices, trellis staking, and soil testing.
Tomato_healthy.organic_treatment: Apply compost mulch and beneficial mycorrhizal root inoculants.
Tomato_healthy.prevention: Prune lower leaves that touch soil to prevent splash inoculation.
precautions: Prune lower leaves touching the ground to eliminate splash corridors from soil microbes.
Maintain consistent, deep watering to prevent blossom end rot and stress-induced susceptibility.
Inspect leaf undersides and terminal growth twice weekly for early signs of hornworms, mites, or whiteflies.
Apply organic mulch around the stem base leaving 2 inches of breathing room around the main stem.
